title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking Suite, and Runbooks
author: Aisha Natarajan
content:
Summary
-------
This document is the canonical reference for Redwood's serving runtime: runtime architecture, kernel selection and scheduling design, profiling/playbook guidance, benchmarking suite and accepted baselines, release notes for recent runtime changes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers responsible for runtime development, SRE, oncall responders, performance reviewers, and partners onboarding runtime behavior expectations.

Scope
-----
- Components: inference runtime process, kernel selector, request router, KV/Prefix cache, batching subsystem, telemetry hooks, and model adapter layer.
- Environments: hosted (multi-tenant), dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and private (VPC/on-prem) deployments.
- Audience: runtime engineers, infra SRE, performance QA, model-onboarding engineers.

1) High-level Runtime Architecture
--------------------------------
Short intro: The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine providing low-latency, high-throughput token generation. The core responsibilities are model execution, KV-cache management, batching and scheduling, kernel selection, and exposing observability hooks.

Architecture diagram (textual):
- Ingress (API Gateway) -> Router (policy-based routing: latency/cost/region) -> Request Queue
- Request Queue -> Batcher -> Kernel Scheduler -> GPU Execution (model kernels) -> KV Cache -> Egress
- Sidecar services: Metrics exporter, Tracing agent, Model artifact manager, Health & readiness probes

Key invariants:
- Stateless request handling outside of KV cache (to enable routing/fallbacks).
- Kernel selection is per-model-version + workload-profile (sequence length distribution, temperature/stop behavior).
- Batcher enforces latency SLOs with adaptive batching and priority lanes for low-latency customers.

Ownership and components: (owners in parentheses)
- Kernel selector + scheduling (serving-runtime team)
- Batcher (serving-runtime + eng-sre)
- KV/Prefix cache (serving-runtime)
- Observability hooks & telemetry (eng-platform)

SLOs and targets (internal):
| Metric | Target | Notes |
|--------|--------|-------|
| p50 token latency | < 10ms | small models (<= 2B) |
| p95 token latency | < 120ms | typical 8k context models; SLA-backed customers may be tighter |
| throughput (tokens/sec per GPU) | baseline per model in benchmark suite | see Benchmarking section |
| availability | 99.95% | Dedicated clusters SLA |

2) Kernel Scheduling Design
---------------------------
Goals: maximize GPU utilization while meeting latency SLOs and avoiding head-of-line blocking.

Components and behavior:
- Kernel Catalog: mapping of model ops (attention, matmul, softmax) -> optimized kernels (cuBLAS, CUTLASS, Triton kernels, vendor-specific tuned kernels).
- Scheduler inputs: pending batches, batch sizes, sequence length distribution, model variant (quantized/FP16/INT8), GPU memory pressure, affinity pins.
- Priority lanes: low-latency, best-effort, off-peak batch.
- Preemption: for single-token-critical requests we support preemptive scheduling of in-flight kernels when native hardware preemption is available; otherwise we use short preemptible micro-batches (default max 8 tokens).

Kernel selection policy (summary):
1. If model is quantized (INT8/4bit) and sequence length <= 1k, prefer quantized fused-kernels.
2. For long sequences (>1k) prefer kernels with optimized KV streaming and memory tiling.
3. If GPU utilization < 40% and many small requests queue up, enable latency-oriented kernel path that favors smaller batch sizes.

Example kernel decision table:
| Condition | Selected Kernel Type | Rationale |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------|
| small model, short seq, quantized | fused-INT8-kernel | best cost/latency |
| large model, long seq | streaming-KV-kernel | avoids OOM, reduces memory copies |
| many small concurrent requests | low-latency micro-batching kernel | reduces head-of-line latency |

Config knobs (examples):
- max_batch_size: 256
- microbatch_max_tokens: 8
- preemptible_microbatch_timeout_ms: 5
- kernel_selector_mode: auto | latency_first | throughput_first

3) Profiling Playbook (how to profile and triage performance regressions)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Objective: standardize how to capture reproducible performance traces, extract root cause, and assign remediation.

Before you start: reproduce the issue in a controlled environment (staging/dedicated cluster). Ensure deterministic inputs (prompt sets) and model version pinned.

1) Capture baseline + current traces:
- Collect traces for 5–10 representative requests, including cold and warm paths.
- Enable verbose telemetry for the run: 
  - Metrics: per-kernel latency histogram, GPU utilization, memory alloc/free counts, NCCL stats.
  - Traces: in-process spans (scheduler->kernel->copy), host-to-device transfer events.
  - OS: dmesg/syslog for OOM/kern messages.

2) Tools and commands (examples):
- nvidia-smi dmon/power: monitor GPU utilization and memory in real-time.
- nvprof / Nsight Systems: capture GPU kernel timelines (preferred for complex memory/copy issues).
- triton-profiler (if using Triton kernels) to inspect kernel launch parameters.
- perf / eBPF (for host-side scheduling contention)
- runtime built-in trace: POST /internal/trace?request_id=... returns JSON timeline (see sample below)

3) Sample profiling workflow:
1. Reproduce the request set and log request IDs.
2. Run Nsight Systems capture for 30–60s for the workload.
3. Export capture and inspect: kernel launch time, kernel duration, cudaMemcpy times, and idle gaps.
4. Correlate gaps with scheduler decisions and batch formation timestamps.
5. If high cudaMemcpy observed, investigate KV cache misses or model artifact copies; check model pinned to GPU.
6. If long kernel durations: check kernel type chosen and fallback paths (FP16 fallbacks, synchronization barriers).

4) Common root causes & checks:
- High latency spikes: head-of-line blocking from large batch; check batch size histogram.
- GPU memory OOMs: verify quantization profile and peak seq length; check memory fragmentation stats.
- Low throughput with high utilization: kernel-generated excessive synchronization (barriers)/small launches; review kernel launch count per token.
- Telemetry gaps: missing spans due to rate-limiting; enable debug-mode traces for short window.

4) Benchmarking Suite and Baselines
----------------------------------
Purpose: provide reproducible perf numbers used for releases and model onboarding. The suite is the single source of truth for model baselines (latency, throughput, memory footprint, cost-per-token).

Components:
- harness/ (open-source-like harness used by eng teams)
  - workload definitions: interactive-chat, streaming-completion, text-embedding, long-context-generation
  - scenarios: cold-start, steady-state, bursty, long-running sequences
- metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 token latency, tokens/sec per GPU, memory high-water-mark, kernel counts, energy/power where available

Representative baseline table (example):
| Model | Context | p95 token latency | tokens/sec per GPU | notes |
|-------|---------|-------------------|---------------------|-------|
| redwood-7b | 2k | 48ms | 1,200 | quantized INT4 path |
| redwood-13b | 4k | 92ms | 860 | FP16 tuned kernels |
| bloom-176b | 8k | 360ms | 120 | long sequence streaming required |

Benchmark run cadence:
- Nightly quick-suite (smoke): small workloads to detect regressions.
- Weekly full-suite: full-model matrix across hardware types (A100, H100, L40s).
- Release candidate suite: full-suite + customer-specific workloads before rollout.

How to add a new model to the suite (short):
1. Add model artifact to model registry and provide model signature.
2. Add model-to-kernel-mapping with initial heuristics.
3. Run full-suite in staging and record baseline.
4. Peer review baseline and add to catalog.

5) Release Notes (selected runtime changes)
-----------------------------------------
v2026.02.10 (published 2026-02-10)
- Kernel selector: improved heuristics for mixed-sequence workloads (up to 18% p95 improvement on 13B models).
- Batcher: added priority-lane preemption and microbatching mode.
- Fix: resolved KV cache leak causing memory growth under heavy streaming loads.
- Observability: added per-kernel telemetry tags and per-request kernel_trace_id.

v2025.12.03
- Introduced INT4 fused kernels for many attention sizes (experimental, opt-in).
- Improved host-to-device pipelining for model loads; reduced cold-start by ~30%.

6) Known Issues (active)
----------------------
- Memory fragmentation on long-running dedicated nodes with mixed model sizes. Workaround: periodic restart cronjob (service-restart-scheduler) and vacuum script (see runbook). Status: mitigation applied; long-term allocator changes scheduled.
- Intermittent p99 token latency spikes when many small (<16 token) requests arrive concurrently on specific kernel paths. Workaround: enable low-latency microbatching flag. Status: investigating improved preemption.
- INT4 kernels on H100 show rare numerical instability for a small subset of models (reported by model-onboarding). Workaround: fallback to INT8/FP16 for impacted model versions. Status: monitored; patch in progress.

7) Operational Runbooks
----------------------
A) High p95 token latency (serving-runtime)
1. Triage: check the runtime dashboard for affected clusters / model versions.
2. Identify if it is: (a) spike affecting all models on node, (b) specific model.
3. If (a): check GPU utilization, OOMs, dmesg, and network egress saturation. Notify oncall-eng-sre.
4. If (b): check batch size histogram and kernel_trace_id for a sample request.
5. Remediations (in order):
   - Toggle microbatching to latency-first: /bin/runtime-admin set-config --cluster <c> --key kernel_selector_mode=latency_first
   - Scale up dedicated pool (if autoscaler does not react): /bin/infra scale-pool --cluster <c> --delta +2
   - For persistent kernel regressions, rollback kernel selector to previous release: /bin/runtime-admin rollback-kernel-selector --release <tag>
6. Post-incident: collect full Nsight captures and file a regression issue with profiling artifacts attached.

B) GPU OOM / process crash
1. Check node logs and dmesg. If OOM killer invoked, identify process and model.
2. If model artifact load caused OOM: ensure model is pinned correctly and use artifact-cache to warm with smaller batch.
3. If fragmentation suspected: restart the runtime process after draining (use drain endpoint).
4. For repeated OOMs: pin model to larger-GPU instance type or enable streaming-KV kernels.

C) Degraded throughput with high GPU utilization
1. Run perf/eBPF to identify host-side stalls (I/O or mutex contention).
2. Inspect kernel launch rate: excessive small kernels indicate suboptimal kernel selection.
3. Flip kernel_selector_mode=throughput_first for non-SLA customers or schedule a kernel-selector rollout.

9) Appendix: common commands and sample configs
---------------------------------------------
Sample runtime config (YAML snippet):

runtime:
  max_batch_size: 256
  microbatch_max_tokens: 8
  preemptible_microbatch_timeout_ms: 5
  kernel_selector_mode: auto
  telemetry_level: normal

Profiler capture command (Nsight Systems):
nsys profile -o /tmp/profile --sample=cpu --cuda-memory-usage --capture-range cstart,cstop --trace=cuda,osrt --idle-timeout=10000 --duration=60s -- /bin/runtime-run-workload --spec workload.json

Quick diagnostic curl to retrieve traces for request: 
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "https://runtime.internal/api/internal/trace?request_id=<id>" | jq .

Contributing & change process
- All changes to kernel_selector and scheduler must be submitted as an ADR and have a benchmark comparison (full-suite) before rollout.
- Feature rollouts use staged canary: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%, with rollback thresholds for p95 and error-rate.
